lead: Software project management is the work of turning a goal into a plan that a team can follow and correct. It uses four linked views: people, product, process and project. Some syllabi call them the four P's. The views are not phases; they are lenses on the same job. A one-page plan joins them: what is in scope, who does it, how it is built and checked, and what it may cost in time and money. Teams use this in small college builds and in large paid projects, because a schedule without scope or people is guesswork.
prereq: You need Unit 1, Foundations: Software and Process Models, especially process models and the reasons projects fail.

blocks.text: The management spectrum says a manager looks at four things at once. Skipping one view hides a problem that appears later as delay or rework.

items: People: the roles, skills and communication the work needs. A team of six may have one Android developer, one tester, one designer and three developers. Name who owns each task.
Product: the scope and features of what is built. Write what the first release includes and what it leaves out.
Process: the tasks and reviews that turn requirements into tested software. A weekly build and a review at week 5 are process choices.
Project: the plan and control that keep scope, schedule and cost visible. A spend check at week 6 is a project control.

blocks.text: The four P's are views of one project, not four phases. People do product work through a process under project control. Change one view and the plan changes. If a tester is missing, product scope may shrink; if scope grows, the process needs more reviews and the project needs more money.

sections.h3: From views to a one-page plan

blocks.text: The plan is one page, not a binder. It states the boundary and the checks that prove the work is done.

items: Write the product scope: first-release features, deferred features and the acceptance test.
Check feasibility: technical, schedule and cost. A payment gateway has a different cost from a static menu page.
List tasks from the process: design, build, test and review. Add an owner to each task.
Estimate effort and cost with decomposition (breaking work into tasks) or COCOMO (an empirical cost model); see 6.3.
Schedule tasks and find the critical path, the longest chain of dependent tasks that sets the finish date; see 6.4.
Write the risk plan: top risks, probability, impact and response; see 6.5.
Set the baseline and control: weekly status, approved changes and replanning; see 6.2 for metrics and 6.6 for version control of work products.

blocks.text: A one-page plan is enough for a small team because it names the scope, the tasks, the dates, the money and the person who checks each item. Detailed charts come later.
Control compares plan with fact. The approved plan is the baseline; the status gives actual values. A variance is a difference that needs a decision.
planned spend by week k = B × k ÷ N
blocks.where: B is total budget in rupees; N is number of weeks; k is the week number from 1 to N; spend is in rupees.

blocks.text: This assumes an even spend across weeks; if spend is uneven, add the weekly planned amounts up to week k instead.

For B = ₹40,000 and N = 10, planned spend by week 6 is 40,000 × 6 ÷ 10 = ₹24,000. If actual spend is ₹29,000, the project is ₹5,000 over the planned spending line — a cost overrun, not progress. Spending above plan only looks acceptable if the work finished is also ahead; here the manager must check scope or cost.

Control points differ by view. People: a skills gap or an overloaded member. Product: a new feature that was not in scope. Process: a review that finds many defects. Project: spend, date or a missed milestone. Each control point needs an owner, a date and a pass condition. If a check fails, replan the one page; do not hide the failure in a status report.
Monitoring is not the same as testing. Testing checks the product; monitoring checks the plan. A weekly build can pass tests while the schedule slips.

figure.caption: The four views feed one plan; the plan is executed and monitored, and a failed check returns to replanning.

spec.title: Four P's to plan
spec.aria: The four P's feed a project plan, which is executed, monitored and replanned.

examples.question: A college team of 6 students has 10 weeks and ₹40,000 to build a hostel mess app with 8 must-have features. Write the four P's and give one control point for each. Also compute the number of features deferred if the first release keeps 5, the average budget per week, and the planned cumulative budget at week 6 and week 10.
steps: People: the 6 students are 1 Android developer, 1 tester, 1 designer and 3 developers. Control point: a week-1 skills check with a named owner for each task.
Product: 8 must-have features. The first release keeps 5. Deferred features = 8 − 5 = 3. Control point: a scope review before week 5.
Process: weekly build and review at week 5. Control point: the week-5 review checks build, test and defect count.
Project: budget ₹40,000 over 10 weeks. Average spend per week = 40,000 ÷ 10 = ₹4,000. This assumes an even spend across weeks; if spend is uneven, add the weekly planned amounts up to week 6 instead.
Planned spend by week 6 = 6 × ₹4,000 = ₹24,000. Planned spend by week 10 = 10 × ₹4,000 = ₹40,000. Control point: spend checks at week 6 and week 10.
Put the four control points into the one-page plan, each with owner, date and pass condition.
examples.answer: The first release defers 3 features, spends ₹4,000 per week on average, ₹24,000 by week 6 and ₹40,000 at week 10.
examples.check:
total_budget = 40000
weeks = 10
features = 8
kept = 5
deferred = features - kept
per_week = total_budget / weeks
week6 = per_week * 6
week10 = per_week * 10
print(deferred)
print(per_week)
print(week6)
print(week10)

traps: Starting with a schedule before product scope: a date cannot define features.
Treating the four P's as phases; they are views used together on one project.
Confusing process control with project control: a design review is process; a spend check is project.
Forgetting people: adding tasks without owners makes a plan that cannot be executed.
Using actual spend alone; compare it with planned spend by week, or a low spend can hide slow work.

quiz.q: Name the four P's of the management spectrum.
Why are the four P's called views and not phases?
quiz.a: They are four lenses on the same project at the same time. Work does not finish people and then start product; changes in one view change the others.

quiz.q: A team has 8 features and the first release keeps 6. The budget is ₹50,000 over 5 weeks. Find the deferred features, spend per week and planned spend by week 3.
quiz.a: Deferred = 8 − 6 = 2 features. Spend per week = 50,000 ÷ 5 = ₹10,000. Planned spend by week 3 = 3 × 10,000 = ₹30,000.

quiz.q: A project is on date, but scope has grown and the only tester is shared with another team. Which views show risk, and why?
quiz.a: Product shows scope growth; People shows the shared tester and skills risk; Project shows the effect on date and cost. Process may also need more reviews. The date alone hides these risks.

quiz.q: What is the first planning step in the one-page plan?
quiz.a: Write the product scope: first-release features, deferred features and acceptance test.

quiz.q: Why check feasibility before making a detailed task list?
quiz.a: A detailed plan for an impossible product wastes effort. Feasibility checks technical, schedule and cost limits before tasks are fixed.

quiz.q: A plan has a design review at week 5 and a spend check at week 6. Classify each control point.
quiz.a: The design review is a process control point. The spend check is a project control point.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same four views appear as a project charter, product backlog, delivery process and earned-value control. Many teams keep a one-page plan and update it in a weekly review. Product managers own scope, engineering managers own process, and project managers own cost and date. Search for project charter, earned value management, product discovery and risk register to go deeper.
